title: Searching a graph
summary: Visit neighbors of neighbors, and remember where you've been so loops don't trap you.

say.never: Picture exploring a building you've never seen. You walk into a room, note every door, and pick one to try. To be sure you don't walk in circles forever, you chalk an X on each room as you enter. If a room already has an X, you turn around. Searching a graph works the same way. The X is a `Set` of nodes you've **visited**.
say.bit: Search by visiting neighbors of what you've reached. Keep a **visited** `Set`, or a loop traps you.

marks.label: rooms with an X on them

steps.title: A stack of doors to try

say.never: Keep the doors you still have to try on a **stack**, like a pile of plates: `push` puts one on top, `pop` takes the top one off. Pop a room, skip it if it's chalked, chalk it, and push each of its doors. When the pile is empty, you've seen every room you can get to. Going as deep as you can before backing up is called a **depth-first search**. Java's `ArrayDeque` makes a good stack.
say.bit: A **depth-first search**: `push` the start; loop `pop`, skip if visited, mark it, `push` its neighbors.

steps.title: In your lesson: A stack of doors to try

say.never: `canReach` is that search. Start at `from`, and if you ever pop `to`, the answer is `true`. If the stack runs out first, it's `false`. Check the edge cases first: a waypoint not on the map (use `containsKey`) can't reach or be reached. `unreachable` can use the same search: when it ends, every waypoint *not* in the visited set is cut off.
say.bit: `canReach`: search from `from`, `true` if you pop `to`. `unreachable`: search from `start`, list what isn't visited, sorted.
